Calm your tits. If you took 0.25 seconds to google it (ha funny), you'd see that the Linux foundation already has signing rights and will distribute a bootstrappable signed loader so you can load whatever Linux distro you want. Source

I'm well aware of that.

I'm also aware that they themselves refer to their prior boot loaders as a stopgap, and I don't know that this is necessarily going to be much different. I somehow doubt that this will be allowed to persist forever. And end-users signing precompiled kernels isn't going to happen. Plus, having a signed bootloader being able to load a kernel seems like a good way to essentially have malware use it to boot into memory somehow. I admit I don't know all the details on this process, but I could pretty easily see it happening and result in a pretty big hole in the security this would provide.

So no, I'm not going to "calm my tits." The fact that you can't turn it off on tablets, and that mainstream PC makers are allowed to make it impossible to disable, gives quite a bit of indication where we're headed with this. Should it play out, it's not going to happen... right away.

That said, I'm pretty sure people would be a lot more unhappy with the spying if we hadn't been spied on by Google for so many years. It's a gradual acclimation. Much as Windows 10's data collection wouldn't have flown nearly so well 10 years ago, the slow and gradual tightening shows no signs of slowing down.
A stopgap is exactly what you need if you just want to, well, stop a gap. Which is exactly what it does.

So far as I am aware, a stopgap is generally meant to stop a gap on a temporary basis until a more permanent solution can be implemented. The permanent solution for this is "talk Microsoft into revising the specifications," but it's not too likely that'll happen. Instead there will be a number of kernels that may be signed, probably pre-designated by commercial elements of the Linux community for the most part - mostly the ones that are slipping monetization akin to the Ubuntu controversies over search results and Firefox's various concerning moves as of late. I do not find this an attractive solution, and I am rather certain I'm not alone in this evaluation.

If this particular boot loader continues being usable far into the future and can be used as a stepping off point for other OS's, then that's great. But Microsoft's behavior throughout the design of Windows 10 has been extremely concerning to myself and a large number of people, and for good reason. Add in the fact that most of this sort of thing ends up being progressively adopted so as to get people used to the idea before they go further, and that we're rapidly reaching the point where the software companies own your computer more than you do (we may already be there!), and their prior behavior as a company, and you have yourself a situation that's ripe for some rather serious trouble once things are nailed down enough that there is little that can be done about them.

I agree with you that, from the free software dev perspective, it's not as ideal as our current "CPU runs whatever you feed it" model. What I meant by "it stops a gap", though, is that any tiny window of opportunity is enough to allow free code into a system. An officially recognized, legitimate, legal doorway allowing unsigned code to execute if the owner of the hardware desires it to is entirely sufficient.

Note that, if I'm reading it right, it's the boot loader that requires signing, not any subsequent code. So as long as there's an unrestricted boot loader available there's no issue for the dev community.

I remember a time when the mouse was a foreign and strange input device. I thought it cumbersome and inconvenient to move my hand from the keyboard to move the cursor when I could do it so much faster with the arrow keys. Now my resting position is left hand WASD and right hand on the mouse no matter what I'm doing.

I remember the release of 3.0, and solitaire really did help a lot of people learn to use the mouse. Funny to think about it now, but I remember one woman in particular in our office who could just not figure it out. She ended up taping her mouse to the side if her monitor to get it out of her way.
When I read the title, I got what it was saying. It all just clicked into place. Goddamnit.. Microsoft of ye olde times were smart. I stand humbled by the programmers of the past.

It make even more sense, when you think that the purpose NOW is to get user away from the mouse and into the touchscreen habit.

Unfortunately their success in making me appreciate the mouse make me see touchscreen input as clumsy and inefficient .. or may be it really is clumsy.
All that and I still don't understand Minesweeper.

This Leverletto was made by AKC, the same folks who make so many of the Italian Stiletto-style autos. It was designed by Bill DeShivs and is, to my eye at least, built to a slighter nicer standard than the usual run-of-the-mill stilettos.

The copy is just a copy. It looks pretty good in the photos but in the hand, you can see the extra shortcuts that were taken. It opens at about half the speed of the real one, too.

The Leverletto is a nice design, and with a better steel for the blade it would make a nice, if somewhat pointy, EDC. As I mentioned in my earlier Mikov post, leaf-spring lever locks have the advantage of safer carry, more ergonomic deployment, and ease of one-hand closing. I have read that the leverletto "has the option to be used as a folder or fully automatic with the turn of a set screw" but I have yet to remember to actually try to find this screw whenever I happen to have the knife at hand. I can say it opens quickly with a satisfying whack, locks solidly into place, and has no blade play once it is there.

The only thing holding me back is the steel. As you can see I have not sharpened my example, but everything I has read on the topic says that the unspecified 440 stainless is the usual soft stuff found on knives which were not really intended to hold a good cutting edge. It seems pointless to ruin the factory edge on a knife that would be slated to live in the safe no matter what. If they made a version with a better blade I'd buy it, and I'd carry it too.

They also make a mini version with a smooth front bolster instead of a cross guard, a design I'd prefer in the larger knife as well. It has a trim, efficient appearance that seems to suit it. You can see a nice arraignment of many of the varieties here:

http://mikovknives.com/Italian/italian.html

The copy - I have no idea who made it - was something I picked up because it was cheap, and it lead me to discover the real thing. If it had the blade etch it would probably fool many of the people who would handle it, which would be a shame, as it won't hold a candle to the real one.
